newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bonds dive more than one full point.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bonds dive more than one full point.

text.p: Spanish bonds fell more than a full point in the afternoon following in the footsteps of Italian Btps, dealers said.

They said a wave of pessimism on European monetary Union could be the reason but others added that they saw a simultaneous sell-off in the European peripheral markets and a rise in Swiss money market rates.

"It could be that one or two big players decided to unwind their positions both on Italy and on Spain," a dealer in London said. December futures fell 122 basis points to 106.28, supports are seen at 106/106.15.
"I do not see any particular reason for this sell-off, but rather a technical market," said Jose Ramon Nunez, dealer at Benito y Monjardin in Madrid.
The Spanish market has risen almost steadily in the last three months amid growing optimism about possible entry of Spain to the European Monetary Union from the start in 1999.
The 10-year spread over German Bunds had fallen from 440 basis points in September 1995 to almost 150 a week ago. Today it went back to 182.
"After such a big rise it is normal to see a kind of correction," Nunez added.

Other dealers in London said that it was likely big players decided to unwind their positions. Swiss money market rates rose even though the Swiss National Bank said this tightness is not the result of any policy change.
"It could prove more expensive than before for any U.S. investment fund to keep open a position," a London dealer said. "And it seems less likely to gain than it was in the past."
But the peseta was little affected, trading at 84.10/12 versus the mark from 84.07/09, while the lira was at 998.10/40 from 992.15/20.
Still convinced that a correction was long overdue, dealers adedd that this drop should not bring a market turnaround.
"I am sure the market has too much liquidity at this point," said Alessandro Ceccaroni, managing director at UBS in London "but I do not believe this is going to be a turnaround point".
